b: Prebid Server is open-source software that runs header bidding auctions on a remote server instead of inside a web browser or mobile app. A page, app or video player sends one request to the server; the server forwards bid requests to many demand partners at once, collects their answers and returns the results to the publisher's ad server. It exists because running every auction on the user's device is slow and, in some environments such as connected TV, impossible. Prebid.org's documentation describes it in one line: "an open-source solution for server-to-server header bidding."
It is one of three main products in the Prebid family, alongside the browser library Prebid.js and the Prebid Mobile software development kit (SDK).
How an auction runs through Prebid Server

The sequence starts on the client. That client can be Prebid.js on a web page, the Prebid Mobile SDK in an app, an Accelerated Mobile Pages (AMP) page, or a server-side ad insertion system for long-form video. Instead of calling each supply-side platform (SSP) separately, the client sends a single request to a Prebid Server endpoint.

The main entry point is /openrtb2/auction. According to Prebid.org's endpoint documentation, it "runs an auction with the given OpenRTB 2.x bid request." OpenRTB, short for Open Real-Time Bidding, is the IAB Tech Lab's standard format for bid requests and responses. Prebid's FAQ describes the auction as "basically just OpenRTB 2.6, but with quite a few Prebid-specific extensions." Those extensions sit under an ext.prebid object and control targeting keys, caching, stored requests, bid adjustment factors and price floors.

Processing then happens in three stages, according to the Prebid Server overview. First, the server validates and enriches the request. It can pull a stored request - a saved configuration held on the server, so that a mobile app does not need to ship its full bidder setup in every call - and it applies privacy rules before anything leaves the server. Second, it calls bidders through server-side bid adapters, of which the documentation lists more than 230. Third, it assembles the response: converting currencies, rounding prices into buckets for ad server targeting and, for video and AMP, storing creatives or VAST (Video Ad Serving Template) markup in a companion service called Prebid Cache.

The response returns targeting keys that an ad server such as Google Ad Manager can read. With includewinner set, the server returns hb_pb (the price bucket), hb_size and hb_bidder. With includebidderkeys, it returns per-bidder versions such as hb_pb_BIDDER. Other keys include hb_cache_id and hb_deal.

Time is the scarcest resource. The OpenRTB field tmax tells bidders how many milliseconds they have; the sample request in Prebid's documentation uses 500. Prebid guidance sets the server timeout below the overall page timeout, defaulting to 75%, as described in PPC Land's explainer on wrappers, which cites a recommended range of 50% to 75%. On the Java version, bidder timeouts are bounded by a configured minimum of 50 milliseconds and a maximum of 5,000 milliseconds by default, according to the endpoint documentation.
The cookie problem and user syncing

A server has no access to the browser's cookie jar. That single fact drives much of Prebid Server's design. To let bidders recognise a user, Prebid Server keeps its own record of bidder user IDs, built through a /cookie_sync endpoint. The endpoint returns sync pixels for the browser to fire, and each bidder writes its ID back to a cookie on the host's domain. A userSyncLimit setting caps how many syncs run per page; AMP uses max_sync_count.

The results are weaker than client-side matching. Patrick McCann, senior vice president of research at Raptive and chair of Prebid.js, told AdExchanger in December 2023 that third-party cookies used server-side carry a weaker signal because of the intermediary server. The PPC Land header bidding explainer notes that Index Exchange documentation says its browser adapter matches users better than its server path. Alternative identifiers such as Unified ID 2.0 travel in the user.ext.eids array to compensate.
Who builds it and who runs it

Prebid Server exists in two code bases. The original is written in Go. According to Prebid.org, Rubicon Project (now Magnite) ported it to Java "because they had more engineers who knew Java than Go." Both run in production, and Prebid keeps their external interfaces identical while allowing small functional gaps. New bid adapters are built in Go first and ported to Java "within a couple of months," according to the documentation, which also recommends the Go version for long-form video. As of November 2026, the Go project's Go module is published at major version 4, with v4.11.1 the latest release listed on newreleases.io.

Prebid.org distinguishes hosted Prebid Server, operated by a Prebid.org member company, from self-hosting, which it says is "not nearly as easy as Prebid.js." The documentation names two typical operators: "tech-savvy publishers" and managed service providers. In practice the operators are mostly SSPs and publisher monetisation firms. By one account cited in PPC Land's Prebid explainer, SSPs manage more than 90% of server-side installations.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) publishes deployment guidance which it says handles 5,000 to 100,000 requests per second, with an idle deployment in its US East region costing about $291 a month as of November 2026, before any traffic.

AppNexus announced Prebid Server on May 3, 2017, in New York, describing it as "a server-side header bidding solution available free to publishers." The release named Facebook as a demand source and said Index Exchange and PubMatic would follow. Michael Richardson, senior director of product line management at AppNexus, said the product gave publishers access to "the largest header bidding marketplace and premium demand sources."

At that point Prebid was still an AppNexus-led project. Prebid.org launched as an independent organisation on September 11, 2017, and Prebid.js 1.0 followed on December 13, 2017, according to PPC Land's header bidding explainer. Prebid Server reached AMP through the Real-Time Config integration in February 2018.

Heather Carver, chief revenue officer at Freestar, told AdExchanger that server-side header bidding "was born primarily from the sell side's desire to reduce page load times." Over time the use cases widened to apps, connected TV, digital out-of-home and audio. The Prebid Mobile SDK runs in more than 2,000 apps, as reported in PPC Land's coverage of SDK 3.0, where Teads said it could already serve demand through the standard Prebid Server integration.

The Go code base's move to version 4 brought breaking changes listed in the release notes: the legacy /openrtb2/video endpoint was marked deprecated, embedded root certificates were dropped in favour of system certificates, and several adapters were removed or renamed.

For publishers, Prebid Server is the main open-source alternative to closed server-side auctions run by ad servers or exchanges. Carver said publishers can add "an almost unlimited number" of SSPs server-side, while McCann put the practical client-side ceiling at eight to 12 SSPs.

For buyers, the server is often where a bid request is born. That makes it the place where supply path data, consent strings and identifiers are attached or lost. PPC Land reported that Prebid's August 27, 2025 decision to stop passing cross-exchange transaction IDs particularly affected publishers using Prebid Server, where implementation options were limited.

Its importance grew in 2026 through antitrust. On September 2, 2026, Judge Leonie Brinkema ordered Google to build integrations that open AdX and DFP to Prebid on "functionally equivalent" terms, according to PPC Land's report on the unsealed ruling. The ruling refers to Prebid as a framework rather than naming Prebid Server specifically, so how the integration will be split between browser and server code is not yet settled.

Three criticisms recur. The first is identity loss: lower cookie match rates mean server-side bids are often priced lower than the same bidder's client-side bids, which is why many publishers run a hybrid of both. The second is transparency. Carver noted that SSPs get less visibility into server-side auctions, and every bidder must trust the host's handling of the auction. The third is concentration. Although the code is open, hosting is dominated by SSPs that are also bidders in the same auctions, which raises questions about neutrality.
Cost is also raised: Dennis Colon, head of product and strategy at JIFFY.ai, told AdExchanger that server-side setups are more expensive.
How it differs from adjacent terms

Prebid.js is the browser library. It can run auctions entirely on the page or hand some bidders to Prebid Server through its server-to-server configuration. Header bidding is the technique of calling multiple demand sources before the ad server decides; Prebid Server is one way to implement it, not a synonym. A wrapper is the container code that manages a header bidding auction; Prebid Server turns the wrapper into a single call that fans out on the server. Google's Open Bidding (formerly Exchange Bidding) is a proprietary server-side auction inside Google Ad Manager, while Prebid Server is open-source and can be run by any operator.

Prebid.org's agenda in 2026 has moved toward AI buying. In January 2026 it took over the Prebid Sales Agent repository from AgenticAdvertising.org, as PPC Land reported in its coverage of the open-source sales agent, listing Prebid Server among the projects the organisation manages. IAB Tech Lab's Trusted Server project, an edge-computing layer for ad serving, now routes server-side auctions to Prebid Server using an OpenRTB 2.6 profile with a default timeout of 1,000 milliseconds. And the Google remedies have put Prebid at the centre of how AdX demand reaches publishers. PubMatic chief executive Rajeev Goel said Google's own engineers estimate the integration will take roughly a year to 15 months.

Who: Prebid.org maintains Prebid Server. AppNexus created it, Rubicon Project (now Magnite) built the Java version, and SSPs, managed service providers and some large publishers host it.

What: An open-source server that receives one auction request from a page, app or video system, sends OpenRTB bid requests to more than 230 bidders, and returns priced targeting keys to the publisher's ad server.
When: Announced on May 3, 2017; reached AMP in February 2018; the Go version is at v4.11.1 as of November 2026.
Where: On servers operated by host companies or cloud deployments, between the publisher's client (Prebid.js, Prebid Mobile, AMP, CTV ad insertion) and demand partners.

Why: Running every auction on the device slows pages and cannot work in apps, CTV or audio. Prebid Server moves the auction to the server, at the cost of weaker user matching and greater reliance on the host.
